context: The excerpt describes REPLAB benchmarking, but contains no information about ALOHA or other specific low-cost robot-arm benchmarks. REPLAB’s grasping benchmark uses a test set of 20 toys, selected to include feasible stable grasps; objects are varied in shape and size, with approximately half hard plastic and half soft toys. A grasp attempt is generated from a segmented point-cloud object: a cluster is selected, grasp coordinates are sampled around its center, and the angle is randomized or chosen using baseline-specific rules. Testing reports cumulative success rate (CSR), defined as the number of successfully grasped objects versus the number of attempts. The protocol terminates after success or after 10 unsuccessful attempts, followed by sweeping the arm over the workspace floor to perturb objects. The training dataset contains over 92,000 labeled random grasps, collected in parallel on two cells; approximately 23% succeed. For reaching, the task is to control the six joint velocities so the end-effector reaches a specified 3D target. Joint angles and end-effector position are observations, and performance is measured by distance to the target over training time; the per-step reward is negative Euclidean distance. context: The ALOHA ACT experiments evaluated six real-world and two simulated bimanual manipulation tasks. The simulated tasks were Cube Transfer and Bimanual Insertion; the real tasks were Slide Ziploc, Slot Battery, Open Cup, Thread Velcro, Prep Tape, and Put On Shoe. Real-task demonstrations were collected through ALOHA teleoperation: 50 demonstrations per task, except Thread Velcro, which used 100, for approximately 350 real demonstrations total. The simulated experiments recorded 50 successful scripted demonstrations and 50 successful human demonstrations for each task. Real-world results used one training seed and 25 evaluations per task. ACT’s real-task success rates were: Slide Ziploc—92% Grasp, 96% Pinch, 88% Open; Slot Battery—100% Grasp, 100% Place, 96% Insert; Open Cup—100% Tip Over, 96% Grasp, 84% Open Lid; Thread Velcro—92% Lift, 40% Grasp, 20% Insert; Prep Tape—96% Grasp, 92% Cut, 72% Handover, 64% Hang; Put On Shoe—100% Lift, 92% Insert, 92% Support, 92% Secure. Simulated results are reported separately for scripted versus human training: Cube Transfer achieved 97|82, 90|60, and 86|50% across its subtasks; Bimanual Insertion achieved 93|76, 90|66, and 32|20%.

context: Burger et al. used a KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR) arm mounted on a KUKA Mobile Platform (KMP) mobile base. The arm had a maximum payload of 14 kg and an 820 mm reach; the combined robot and base weighed approximately 430 kg, and its movement was restricted to 0.5 m s−1 for safety. The mobile platform’s uncalibrated navigation repeatability/precision was better than ±10 mm in x-y position and less than ±2.5° in orientation. Because this was insufficient for delicate tasks such as vial placement, the researchers applied a touch-sensitive six-point calibration method. This improved positioning accuracy to ±0.12 mm and orientation accuracy to ±0.005°, broadly comparable to a human operator for delicate manipulations. During the autonomous search, the system ran 43 batches of 16 samples, totaling 688 experiments. Eleven results were discarded due to workflow errors or excessive oxygen caused by faulty vial seals, leaving 677 retained experimental results.

The reported task families are binning objects, placing a target next to a referent, placing it between two referents, and moving it toward or up to a boundary object; the evaluation includes one- and four-object bin variants. Success is state-based and must persist for 5 seconds. Bin success requires every object to be inside the bin footprint and untouched; next-to and between use geometric distance/collinearity constraints; move requires forward progress or contact with the object ahead, a path within 2 inches of straight, and minimal boundary-object displacement. context: The SO-101 Bench is a simulated, language-conditioned spatial-manipulation benchmark built using an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It evaluates four core task types—placing an object in a bin, placing one object next to another, placing an object between two reference objects, and moving an object in a specified direction—organized into five task families. Evaluation covers 138 objects divided into seen objects, unseen instances, and unseen classes, with 916 simulated episodes. Performance is reported as mean success across the 15 task-family-by-object-split cells, with additional subsets testing held-out visual appearances (ROBUST), rotate-to-fit planning (PLAN), and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Policies are fine-tuned on 3,629 simulated teleoperation demonstrations under equal compute budgets. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the strongest learned policies achieve about 61% mean success, while spatial placement, novel object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain difficult. An LLM agent that writes manipulation code and delegates grasping to a learned policy reaches 83.2%. The benchmark’s sim-to-real validation reports that five policies trained without real data preserve their exact ranking on the physical SO-101 in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman ρ = 1.00; MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates absolute success.
question: What does the SO-101 Bench paper describe? What tasks, success criteria, number of trials, and results are reported for the SO-101 arm?

context:
The excerpt describes the SO-101 as an open-source, 3D-printed six-servo arm and identifies it as a common entry point for robot learning. It costs approximately $120–150 to build, compared with roughly $4,900 for an ALOHA arm. LeRobot supports the arm throughout the pipeline, from teleoperation to deployment, and SO-100/101 platforms account for a large share of community datasets on Hugging Face. The text also notes that models such as SmolVLA and MolmoAct2 are trained or post-trained on community SO-100/101 data, but are generally starting points requiring task-specific fine-tuning; no released policy is reported to solve spatially constrained, language-conditioned SO-101 tasks out of the box in new environments with new objects.

The cited SO-101 benchmarks are physical-hardware evaluations involving tasks such as insertion, pouring, wiping, spatial grounding, relational placement, referential descriptions, ordinal position, and counting. The introduced SO-101 Bench instead provides simulation with four task types—Bin, Next to, Between, and Move—organized into five task families and evaluated on seen objects, unseen instances, and unseen classes. It reports 916 evaluation episodes and 3,629 simulated demonstrations. The best learned policies score around 61%, while an LLM agent combined with a learned grasping policy reaches 83.2%.
